I read all 19 pages of the Project 3 document.

What they actually want

The main objective is Database Integration.

Unlike Project 2 (where you mainly created APIs), Project 3 expects you to connect your backend to a real database so the data is stored permanently instead of disappearing when the server restarts.

What you need to build

You need to create a Full Stack CRUD application where:

Frontend
      │
      ▼
Express.js Backend
      │
      ▼
MySQL Database

The frontend sends requests to your backend, and the backend stores/retrieves data from MySQL.

What DecodeLabs expects

1. Design a Database Schema

Before coding, create a table.

Example:

Students
--------------------------
id (Primary Key)
name
email
course
age
created_at

The PDF explains that you should understand:

  • Primary Key

  • Foreign Key

  • Relationships

  • Table Design

Even if your project has only one table, you should know these concepts.

2. Connect Backend with Database

Instead of storing data like this:

JavaScript
let students = [];

you must connect Node.js to MySQL.

For example:

Node.js
↓

mysql2

↓

MySQL Database

This is the biggest change from Project 2.

3. Implement CRUD Operations

Your application must support all four CRUD operations.

CRUDHTTPSQL
CreatePOSTINSERT
ReadGETSELECT
UpdatePUT/PATCHUPDATE
DeleteDELETEDELETE

The PDF specifically maps each CRUD operation to its corresponding HTTP method and SQL command.

4. Use REST APIs

You'll need endpoints such as:

GET /students

GET /students/:id

POST /students

PUT /students/:id

DELETE /students/:id

These APIs should communicate directly with the database.

5. Data Validation

The document emphasizes database constraints like:

  • NOT NULL

  • UNIQUE

  • CHECK

  • Primary Key

For example:

  • Email cannot be empty.

  • Two users cannot have the same email.

These constraints help maintain data integrity.

6. Prevent SQL Injection

One page discusses SQL Injection.

❌ Unsafe:

SQL
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE email = '" + input + "'";

✅ Safe:

Use parameterized queries:

JavaScript
connection.query(
"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email=?",
[email]
);

This prevents attackers from injecting SQL commands.

7. Test Everything

You should verify your APIs using Postman.

Test:

  • Create data

  • Read data

  • Update data

  • Delete data

Technologies they expect

The slides mention:

Backend

  • Node.js

  • Express.js

Database

  • MySQL (recommended)

  • PostgreSQL (also discussed)

Driver

Native drivers such as:

mysql2

They also introduce ORMs (Prisma, SQLAlchemy, Mongoose), but they do not require you to use one for this project.

What they teach in the slides

The presentation also explains the theory behind:

  • SQL vs NoSQL

  • One-to-One relationships

  • One-to-Many relationships

  • Many-to-Many relationships

  • Primary Keys

  • Foreign Keys

  • CRUD

  • REST API mapping

  • Native Drivers vs ORM

  • SQL Injection

  • Parameterized Queries

These are learning concepts rather than additional implementation requirements.

My recommendation for our project

Since Project 2 was a Student Management System, we can make Project 3 much stronger by upgrading it instead of starting from scratch.

We'll build a Student Management System with MySQL, including:

  • ✅ React frontend

  • ✅ Express backend

  • ✅ MySQL database

  • ✅ Full CRUD operations

  • ✅ REST APIs

  • ✅ Postman testing

  • ✅ Proper database schema

  • ✅ Parameterized SQL queries

  • ✅ GitHub repository

  • ✅ Demo video

  • ✅ LinkedIn post

This will satisfy every core requirement described in the Project 3 document while giving you a more professional portfolio project.

I suggest we build it step by step, starting with the database setup and then connecting it to your existing backend.

ChatGPT said:

Yes. I have now read and understood the complete 19-page Project 3 document you uploaded. I will treat this PDF as the official requirement for your DecodeLabs Project 3, rather than assuming requirements from Project 2 or general full-stack practices.

Project 3 — What DecodeLabs actually wants

The project is titled:

Project 3: Database Integration

The central purpose is to move from temporary application data to persistent database storage. In other words, your backend must be able to store data in a database and retrieve it later. Page 2 calls this the “persistence phase” and emphasizes Data Longevity.

The four main pillars

Page 6 gives a very useful summary of what they expect:

PillarWhat it means
1. The BlueprintSchema & database design
2. The BridgeBackend–database integration/connection
3. The ActionCRUD & RESTful HTTP
4. The ShieldData integrity & security

So the project isn't simply “connect MySQL to Node.js.” They want you to demonstrate these four areas.

1. Database/schema design

You need to design a simple database schema.

The document introduces:

  • SQL / relational databases

  • NoSQL / non-relational databases

  • Tables

  • Primary keys

  • Foreign keys

  • Relationships

Page 7 compares SQL and NoSQL and specifically gives MySQL and PostgreSQL as SQL examples and MongoDB as a NoSQL example.

Relationships they want you to understand

Page 8 explains:

  • One-to-One (1:1)

  • One-to-Many (1:Many)

  • Many-to-Many (M:M)

For M:M, they show that an intermediate/junction table is required.

Keys

Page 9 explains:

Primary Key

  • uniquely identifies each row.

Foreign Key

  • points to a primary key in another table.

  • establishes a relationship between tables.

  • maintains referential integrity.

Important point

They don't say that your project must have a complicated multi-table database.

The explicit requirement on page 4 is:

Design a simple database schema

So we should not unnecessarily make the project complicated just to add tables.

2. Connect your backend to the database

This is the actual core of Project 3.

The required concept is:

Backend
   ↓
Database connection/integration
   ↓
Database

Page 10 explains that application code needs a translation/integration layer to communicate with database storage.

They introduce two approaches:

Native database driver

For example:

Node.js
   ↓
Database Driver
   ↓
Database

This means writing SQL queries yourself.

ORM

They also introduce:

  • Prisma

  • SQLAlchemy

  • Mongoose

The ORM translates database rows into object-oriented code and can provide things such as type safety and autocompletion.

Important: The PDF presents native drivers and ORMs as integration approaches. It does not explicitly say that you must use a particular ORM.

So we should choose the approach based on what best fits your previous project and what allows you to clearly demonstrate the required concepts.

3. CRUD is mandatory

This is one of the clearest requirements.

Page 12 defines:

Create

Add new data.

Read

Retrieve existing data.

Update

Modify existing data.

Delete

Remove unwanted data.

And page 13 maps them directly to the web and database:

OperationHTTPSQL
CreatePOSTINSERT
ReadGETSELECT
UpdatePUTUPDATE
DeleteDELETEDELETE

They also mention PATCH for partial updates.

So our implementation needs to demonstrate that these operations actually work with the database.

4. RESTful API

The CRUD operations aren't supposed to exist only as SQL commands.

They need to be mapped to the web/API layer.

For example, conceptually:

POST    → Create
GET     → Read
PUT     → Update
DELETE  → Delete

The important thing is that:

Frontend/API request
        ↓
Backend
        ↓
Database operation
        ↓
Response

The database should become the persistent source of the application's data.

5. Data integrity — VERY important

This is the part that I don't want us to overlook.

Page 14 says:

The Database is the Final Source of Truth

It specifically introduces database-level constraints:

UNIQUE

Prevents duplicate values.

Example:

email

could be unique.

NOT NULL

Prevents required fields from being empty.

CHECK

Enforces a condition on allowed values.

For example:

age >= 18

The document's point is that data integrity should be enforced at the schema/database level, rather than trusting application logic alone.

So when we design your database, we should deliberately use appropriate constraints.

6. SQL Injection protection — also part of the project

This is another requirement I would take seriously.

Page 15 demonstrates the problem of SQL Injection through malicious user input.

The problem is essentially:

User input
     ↓
directly concatenated into SQL
     ↓
SQL gets manipulated

The document explains that raw string concatenation can allow malicious input to become executable SQL logic.

7. Parameterized queries

Page 16 gives the solution:

❌ Vulnerable

SQL + userInput

✅ Secure

SQL with parameter
        +
user input supplied separately

The PDF calls these Parameterized Queries.

The important idea is:

User input should be treated as data, not executable SQL.

Therefore, when we write your database queries, we should use parameterized queries rather than constructing SQL by directly concatenating user input.

8. What they explicitly say the project goal is

Page 4 is the simplest official summary:

Goal

Connect the backend with a database to store and retrieve data.

Key Requirements

  1. Design a simple database schema

  2. Perform basic CRUD operations

  3. Ensure proper data handling

Key Skills

  • Databases

  • CRUD operations

  • Data storage

That's the core of the assignment.

What is NOT explicitly required

This is important because I don't want us to add unnecessary things.

The PDF does not explicitly require:

  • User authentication

  • JWT

  • Login/register

  • Password hashing

  • Complex authorization

  • A particular frontend framework

  • A particular database

  • A particular ORM

  • A complicated multi-table enterprise system

In fact, page 2 says that before building complex user authentication, you should first master schema design and CRUD.

So we should not turn Project 3 into an authentication project unless there is another DecodeLabs instruction requiring it.

What I think our final project should demonstrate

To satisfy the document properly, our finished project should be able to show:

                 PROJECT 3
                     │
        ┌────────────┴────────────┐
        │                         │
   DATABASE DESIGN          BACKEND INTEGRATION
        │                         │
   Tables / Schema           DB Connection
   Primary Key               Driver / ORM
   Foreign Key
        │                         │
        └────────────┬────────────┘
                     │
                    CRUD
                     │
        ┌────────────┼────────────┐
        │            │            │
      CREATE        READ        UPDATE       DELETE
      POST          GET          PUT         DELETE
        │            │            │            │
        └────────────┴────────────┴────────────┘
                     │
              DATA INTEGRITY
                     │
          UNIQUE / NOT NULL / CHECK
                     │
                  SECURITY
                     │
          Parameterized Queries

That would directly reflect the architecture presented on pages 6, 13, 14 and 16.

One more important thing: Project 3 is a milestone

Page 3 says that completing Project 3 is required to unlock the other projects for the next week, and that projects must be verified for quality. It also describes Project 3 as a definitive milestone for mastering the domain.

And page 18 encourages you to go beyond simply completing it—for example, by optimizing queries or adding data relationships—but those are presented as opportunities to experiment, not as the basic mandatory requirements.

So our priority should be:

First: satisfy every explicit requirement.
Second: make the implementation clean and secure.
Third: add improvements only if they genuinely strengthen the project.

I understand the PDF now, and for the rest of this Project 3 work, I'll use this document as the source of truth for what DecodeLabs is asking you to build.

const borrowingModel = require("../models/borrowingModel");

const getBorrowings = async (req, res) => {
try {
const borrowings = await borrowingModel.getAllBorrowings();
res.json(borrowings);
} catch (error) {
res.status(500).json({ error: error.message });
}
};

const getBorrowing = async (req, res) => {
try {
const borrowing = await borrowingModel.getBorrowingById(
req.params.id
);

    if (!borrowing) {
        return res.status(404).json({
            error: "Borrowing record not found"
        });
    }

    res.json(borrowing);
} catch (error) {
    res.status(500).json({ error: error.message });
}

};

const borrowBook = async (req, res) => {
try {
const { book_id, member_id } = req.body;

    if (!book_id || !member_id) {
        return res.status(400).json({
            error: "book_id and member_id are required"
        });
    }

    const id = await borrowingModel.borrowBook(
        Number(book_id),
        Number(member_id)
    );

    res.status(201).json({
        message: "Book borrowed successfully",
        id
    });
} catch (error) {
    res.status(400).json({
        error: error.message
    });
}

};

const returnBook = async (req, res) => {
try {
await borrowingModel.returnBook(req.params.id);

    res.json({
        message: "Book returned successfully"
    });
} catch (error) {
    res.status(400).json({
        error: error.message
    });
}

};

module.exports = {
getBorrowings,
getBorrowing,
borrowBook,
returnBook
};
